passage: I'm Chinmay. Looking back, the strangest part was the whiplash. In the morning my boss would call my work "the best in the team", and by evening he would say, "Nobody else would hire you, you know that?" I went home dizzy, unable to tell if I was good or hopeless. I stopped seeing friends because he said outside people would distract me. My old college friend Eshaan kept calling anyway. One night Eshaan said, "Send your CV to two places. If he's right, you lose nothing." I did, mostly to prove Eshaan wrong. Both wrote back with interviews. I remember sitting on the bus holding that email and seeing that the praise and the threats were pulling me the same way. I haven't left yet, but I'm no longer only listening to him.

qa.q: What did the boss say about Chinmay's chances of another job?
qa.a: He said nobody else would hire Chinmay.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay feel dizzy by the end of the day?
qa.a: The praise in the morning and the threats by evening left Chinmay unable to tell if the work was good or hopeless.

qa.q: How did Eshaan's suggestion help Chinmay test the boss's claim?
qa.a: Applying to two places tested the claim, and both wrote back with interviews, so the claim was not proven true.

qa.q: How might Eshaan have seen Chinmay's situation from outside?
qa.a: Eshaan kept calling and said Chinmay would lose nothing by applying, which suggests Eshaan saw the claim as untested and worried about Chinmay pulling away from friends.

grounding: A boss alternates praise and threats and says nobody else would hire Chinmay; Chinmay tests the claim by applying elsewhere with an outside friend's help.

passage: Amandeep's month had been a seesaw. On Monday Farhan, who owned the small printing shop in Ludhiana, called him 'my best boy' and bought him lassi. On Wednesday he screamed about a misprint and said, 'Nobody else would hire you. Remember that.' By Friday Amandeep felt dizzy just walking in, as if the floor tilted with Farhan's moods. He had only enough in his pocket for bus fare that week, so quitting felt impossible. On Sunday his old school teacher, Gill-sir, met him at the gurdwara langar and noticed. 'You look like someone holding his breath.' Amandeep told him everything. Gill-sir didn't tell him to quit. 'Test what he says. Apply to two shops. See if it's true.' On Monday Amandeep sent his CV to two printing presses on the same street. One called back that evening for an interview.

qa.q: What did Farhan call Amandeep on Monday?
What was Amandeep feeling by Friday?
qa.a: Amandeep felt dizzy and anxious, as if the floor tilted with Farhan's moods.
Applying to two shops tested Farhan's claim that nobody else would hire him, and the quick callback showed it was false.

qa.q: How does Gill-sir read Amandeep at the langar?
qa.a: Gill-sir sees someone holding his breath, tense and trapped, and cares enough to ask.

grounding: Shows a boss swinging between praise and threats to make Amandeep feel dependent, and testing that claim by applying elsewhere with an outside mentor's help.

passage: Mr. Menon ran the event-management firm in Kochi like the weather. One week he told clients Yash was 'the future of this company'; the next he called Yash into the cabin and said, 'Leave, and I'll make sure no agency in this city touches you. Nobody else would hire you anyway.' Yash, eight months into the job, began to believe it. He stopped telling his elder sister Uma about work because every story sounded like complaining. One Sunday she found him at 1 a.m. still answering Mr. Menon's messages. 'Show me,' she said. He did. She scrolled through a week of it: praise, threat, praise, threat. 'This is a pattern, Yash. And the "nobody would hire you" part is something you can check.' Together they updated his CV that night. By Wednesday he had applied to three agencies, and he had told two college friends what was really going on.

qa.q: How long had Yash been in the job?
qa.a: Yash had been in the job eight months.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when he stopped telling Uma about work?
qa.a: Yash felt ashamed and worn down, afraid every story would sound like complaining.

qa.q: What steps helped Yash see through Mr. Menon's claim?
qa.a: Uma helping him see the praise-threat pattern, updating his CV, applying to three agencies, and telling two friends.

qa.q: What is it like for Uma to find Yash answering messages at 1 a.m.?
qa.a: Uma is worried, and wants to see the messages so she can help him name the pattern.

grounding: Shows a boss alternating praise and threats and claiming nobody else would hire Yash, and his sister helping him spot the pattern and test the claim.
